To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the 3′-end formation of replication-dependent histone genes is regulated in an S-phase-specific manner and that this regulation is mediated by a unique RNA-binding protein, Hrp2.

the 3′ ends of the canonical histone mRNAS are generated by a unique cleavage and polyadenylation process that is regulated by a novel mechanism that involves the interaction of a specific histone pre-mRNA with an RNA binding protein.

the 3′ ends of replication-dependent histone transcripts are formed by cleavage/polyadenylation factors, that this process is regulated in a manner that is coordinated with the replication-dependent synthesis of histone proteins and that this mechanism is evolutionarily conserved.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of gene expression in metazoans.

the mechanisms that control histone mRNA metabolism, with the consequences of this regulation for chromatin structure and gene expression and with the role of these mechanisms in the epigenetic transmission of gene expression patterns.
the regulation of histone gene expression and the role of histone proteins in chromatin structure and transcriptional regulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
histone gene expression is regulated by the coordinated synthesis of the replication-dependent canonical and replication-independent variant histone m RNAs.
the 3′ UTR of the replication-dependent mRNAs is a regulatory element that is required for the rapid synthesis of the histone proteins.

the regulation of histone gene expression is not a single event but a complex process that involves a number of factors that act in a coordinated way to ensure that the correct amount of histone proteins are synthesized at the right time and in the right place.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the histone mRNPs are the first and the last of all mRNAs to be synthesized, and they are the first and last to be degraded.
the 3′ ends of replication-dependent histone mRNA are formed by a process that is distinct from that of other eukaryotic mRNAs, and that this process is subject to regulation.
the regulation of histone mRNA stability and the regulation of histones themselves are not independent processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the synthesis of replication-dependent histones is regulated by the 3′-end structure of their mRNAs.
the regulation of the 3’ end of histone mRNas is a critical aspect of histone gene expression.

the 3′ ends of the replication-dependent mRNAs are not simply a consequence of a lack of a poly(A) polymerase but are instead a consequence of the presence of a specific RNA polymerase II CTD phosphatase.
